items.summary: Anthropic's stock fell roughly 9% from its Nov 19 debut close to a last price of US$88.87 on Nov 20, implying a fully diluted valuation of about US$1.6 trillion (S$2 trillion) and market capitalisation of US$1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding; these figures are the reporter's estimates from trading data rather than company disclosures. The slide reinforced broader AI-trade weakness as Wall Street indexes closed sharply lower on Nov 19 with futures pointing to further declines, while Nvidia and Meta fell more than 2% in premarket trading on Nov 20 and chip stocks including AMD, Sandisk (7% each) and Intel slid more than 5%. Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could buy up to 30% of Anthropic's shares by year-end as potential support. Analysts caution that the roughly 40-times-sales valuation assumes sustained rapid growth; Kaush Amin of US Bank Asset Management urged patience, Rob Hackel of RF Lafferty & Co cited SpaceX's post-IPO volatility and FOMO-driven demand, and Carsten Hesse of Berenberg called the environment unfavourable. Retail investors traded about US$772 million on Nov 19, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking in 2012; this is a reported figure tied to that specific day's data. Attention now turns to OpenAI, which may go public in 2027, and competition from Apple's AI agent reportedly under development as of Nov 20.
items.title: Anthropic's post-debut slide deepens AI-sector gloom

items.summary: Singapore retail investors showed strong appetite for Anthropic on its Nov 19 Nasdaq listing, though analysts flagged valuation worries amid a broader AI-sector selloff. Online brokers reported the stock as the most-traded on its debut day, with trading activity exceeding SpaceX's June session; the six-to-seven-times-oversubscribed IPO raised US$81.3 billion (S$104.8 billion), surpassing SpaceX's US$75 billion raise. Anthropic opened at US$111.50, 34.3% above its US$83 IPO price, briefly exceeded a US$2 trillion intraday market value before closing at US$97.17 with a US$1.8 trillion capitalisation. On Syfe it became the platform's most-traded US stock (about one in four trades), drew more than twice Nvidia's trade count, and saw 83% of orders as market orders versus roughly 65% normally; on Moomoo Anthropic captured around 48% of total trade count and 45% of trading value within its AI/Magnificent Seven basket. Buy activity outpaced sell activity nearly four to one in trade count, suggesting accumulation rather than same-day flipping (attributed by a Moomoo analyst). On Longbridge Securities the stock's trading value was around 4.5 times that of Magnificent Seven stocks on average. Analysts questioned whether first-day momentum could hold: Anthropic closed 17% above its IPO price but well below its opening, and it reported over US$80 billion in losses for H1 2026 (UOB Kay Hian's Kenneth Goh noted much of future success may already be priced in). Morningstar's Lorraine Tan gave a 'Very High' uncertainty rating while citing a 46.5% revenue compound annual growth rate and forecasting capital expenditure peaking in 2028 with positive free cash flow by 2030; she compared the loss-making build-out phase to Amazon, which posted net losses from its 1997 listing until 2003. Syfe's Ganeriwal advised watching volatility as markets settle on value, growth versus cost, and competitor pace (which can shift pricing), while Longbridge Securities' Gavin Chia cautioned that GIC's large stake should not be read as an automatic endorsement of the current valuation, given differing institutional mandates; GIC has invested more than US$4.5 billion across three rounds including a co-led US$65 billion Series H in May, with its stake now worth around US$15 billion at IPO price (Chris Emanuel noted it is now one of Anthropic's largest investors). Separately, Asian markets fell on Nov 20 after Nvidia's Nov 17 earnings: South Korea's Kospi closed 5% lower and Japan's Nikkei 225 also fell 5%, with the Straits Times Index and Hang Seng sliding around 2%, following Wall Street drops of more than 2% in Nasdaq and S&P 500 (Saxo Singapore's Charu Chanana called it a valuation and financing reset rather than an immediate earnings collapse; Ganeriwal pointed to rising expectations of a December US Federal Reserve rate hike as the main driver).
items.title: Anthropic's Singapore retail investor interest and valuation concerns after its record IPO debut

items.summary: Anthropic's Nasdaq listing on Thursday opened at $111.50, peaked at $115 and closed up 17% at $97.17; the article reports this as largely seen by markets as a success for frontier AI firms with no direct peers. On Friday shares fell about 8% to roughly $88, near its IPO price of $83, against broader tech declines: the Nasdaq Composite opened down 1.3%, the S&P 500 down 0.4%, and the Dow largely flat. Anthropic raised a record $81bn in the offering. Analysts attribute expected volatility to the absence of comparable peers and cite SpaceX's large early swings as precedent; Rob Hackel of RF Lafferty & Co said "there's going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX." Early Friday trading was mixed for other US tech names: Tesla down 0.3%, Meta down 1.4% and Nvidia down 2.9%; Europe's Dax fell 2% and the FTSE 100 0.5%. The reported figures are separate facts measuring different things, so no comparison chart is warranted.
items.title: Anthropic shares fell toward its IPO price after a volatile debut amid a tech selloff.

items.summary: On TechCrunch's Equity podcast, hosts Kirsten Korosec, Anthony Ha, and Tim De Chant discussed Nvidia's latest earnings report, which showed healthy growth alongside the company's ongoing handling of its CEO Jensen Huang's departure. The chipmaker announced it would stop selling H200 chips in China and dismissed calls to return Huang as CEO. The discussion also addressed broader AI industry developments, including Anthropic's anticipated public offering and a proposed test of the industry's circular funding model.
items.title: Nvidia reports earnings amid Jensen Huang ouster fallout

items.summary: At an MIT panel titled "AI and Society: The Future of Math," moderated by science writer Kevin Hartnett, mathematicians from MIT, Harvard, Northwestern, and NYU discussed how artificial intelligence is reshaping the field. Panelists Jacopo Borga, Michael Hopkins, Bryna Kra, and Tristan Buckmaster addressed concerns about AI-generated proofs, which they described as lacking human understanding; Hopkins called them "nonsense" containing "strange ideas," while Buckmaster insisted that for math to matter it must have human comprehension. The discussion referenced OpenAI's September announcement of a proof related to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem after 88 hours with thousands of agents, and later released manuscripts dubbed the "mathocalypse." Kra argued priority should no longer be valued, while Hopkins countered that people will still seek pioneering roles; both agreed communication now matters more. Borga questioned whether journals remain the right metric for evaluating mathematicians, noting his journal received a surge in AI-assisted submissions requiring an additional editor and shifting toward valuing exposition over new proofs. Kra highlighted Mathematical Discourse, a video journal emphasizing human aspects of math, while Hopkins pointed to curating older results as another opportunity. Borga cautioned that students are overwhelmed by conflicting guidance amid AI shortcuts, noting his group includes "AI vegans" who avoid the tools; Hopkins described emerging mathematicians skilled at prompting AI for insights. Buckmaster urged students not to abandon mathematics but to find creative and communicative paths forward.
items.title: MIT panel examines AI's impact on mathematical research

items.summary: Khalil Roberts, a 31-year-old New Yorker with over 7,600 followers, tried prompting Meta's Muse AI assistant to identify and unfollow accounts that didn't follow him back. Within minutes it identified 151 accounts via an Excel sheet and he proceeded on November 7; he then posted instructions about the method on X. Over subsequent weeks similar scenarios spread across X, Instagram, and Facebook, with users sharing tips on automating unfollows through Muse. Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 followers, said she used it to find people in real life who had unfollowed her; Elizabeth Brooks prompted the assistant for profile links several times a day so she could manually unfollow accounts from years of sweepstakes promotions. Natalie Pennington, an associate professor at Colorado State University researching social connection, suggested this reflects not wanting to deal with emotionally uncomfortable situations and accessing information that isn't needed. Meta removed an October advertising campaign promoting Muse's promise to show who unfollowed users each week; the company did not respond when WIRED asked about the reasoning behind removing the ad. Roberts said he doesn't plan on letting Muse make more decisions about his social life, drawing a line at unfollowing.
items.title: Users are using Meta's Muse AI assistant to mass-unfollow people who don't follow them back on Instagram.

items.summary: NVIDIA released Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, described by its research team as the first large-scale family of continuous diffusion language models. The collection contains 14 open-source checkpoints at 3B and 8B scale across four variant types: base (Sigma-3B, Sigma-8B), instruct (Sigma-3B-instruct, Sigma-8B-instruct), few-step distilled (distill-3B and distill-8B at NFE 2, 4, 8, 16 for eight checkpoints total), and self-speculative (distill-spec-3B, distill-spec-8B). Unlike discrete-token diffusion models such as LLaDA and Dream, Sigma denoises text in a learned 16-D embedding space using smooth ODE/SDE trajectories. The architecture is a Ministral-style decoder-only Transformer with grouped-query attention, SwiGLU, and rotary embeddings, trained from an autoregressive warm start of about 1T tokens followed by roughly 0.3T diffusion-training tokens; generation runs blockwise in the default 64-token blocks committed to KV cache before each subsequent block. On NVIDIA's own evaluations, Sigma-8B base averaged 71.16 on a six-task suite versus NLD-8B at 70.22, Dream-7B at 58.74 and LLaDA-8B at 41.78; coding led performance with HumanEval at 65.12 versus NLD-8B's 62.80 while MBPP was weaker at 65.74 versus 67.00. After instruction tuning, Sigma-8B-instruct scored 91.96 on GSM8K and 82.50 on HumanEval but averaged only 59.14 across ten tasks, trailing NLD-8B at 59.92, with hard reasoning limited to 23.33 on AIME24 and 17.00 on AIME25; all scores are NVIDIA's own evaluations. The eight-step distilled Sigma-distill-8B-nfe8 averaged 70.34 across six tasks (88.44 GSM8K, 65.18 HumanEval), close to the 256-step teacher, and self-speculative decoding ran about 3.46x faster than autoregressive decoding on one GB200 with SGLang versus NLD-8B's 3.04x average (peak speedups of 4.20x at 8B and 3.18x at 3B). All fourteen checkpoints are available under the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License for commercial use on CUDA GPUs in bfloat16 across Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper and Blackwell architectures; base generation runs about 120 to 140 tokens/s on one H100 with no CPU support or quantized variants listed. The item reports these figures as NVIDIA's own evaluations from the Sigma paper rather than independent verification.
items.title: NVIDIA releases Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a continuous diffusion language model family with 14 checkpoints

items.summary: Elon Musk, who spent $446 million on Republican campaigns nationally during the midterms—roughly half in Texas—included donations to Greg Abbott ($5 million) and Ken Paxton ($10 million), both of whom lost. Democrats instead won control of Congress and major statewide races, prompting Musk at a New York Times DealBook conference to call his spending foolish and predict that incoming Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa would govern as a moderate so "things will be fine in Texas." However, Hinojosa has signaled she may reduce the tax breaks and land deals that attracted Musk's operations. His companies have already received substantial incentives: SpaceX reportedly secured roughly $1.66 billion in potential property tax breaks for its Terafab semiconductor facility in Grimes County—cutting school property taxes by half over 10 years per construction phase—and a $30 million Texas Enterprise Fund grant.
items.title: Musk's Texas political spending failed as Democrats won statewide races and Musk faces a new Democratic governor

items.summary: Starting November 18, Microsoft began automatically upgrading eligible personal and non-managed business devices running Windows 11 24H2 or 25H2 to version 26H2 without manual intervention. The automatic delivery depends on each device's Windows Update settings; managed IT-department machines are excluded from this phase. Devices had already been able to install 26H2 since late October by manually checking for updates, and users can still do so via Settings > Windows Update with the 'Get the latest updates as soon as they're available' option enabled. Microsoft described the change in a release health dashboard update as expanding automatic delivery of what it calls version 26H2's phased rollout; this is presented by the source as fact, though the framing comes from Microsoft itself. The Windows 11 2026 Update became generally available in September 2026 as an enablement package and will reach end of support before October 2029. Separately, Microsoft warned last month that unsupported Windows versions would stop receiving security updates after next year's certificate rotation, and confirmed a hotpatch for devices running Windows 11 24H2 or later is causing installation and launch issues with Office and third-party applications.
items.title: Microsoft begins automatic Windows 11 26H2 upgrades for unmanaged devices

items.summary: Databricks released a public, free, interactive board of reference architectures covering 70 industries across 11 economic sectors as of November 16th 2026. The product is positioned against the common industry-specific redraws of Databricks' ingestion-lakehouse-BI/AI diagram that drifted out of date and lived on individual laptops; this board claims to be updated from the Databricks docs so it does not go stale, with every box opening a panel describing what it is, who uses it, and where to learn more. Each board centers an identical Databricks Platform surrounded by industry-specific sources (964 across all boards as of this blog's release), data formats exchanged (186 in total), teams or personas (1,538), medallion layers using sector terms, and 10 use cases plus 4 Genie Agents, 4 AI/BI dashboards, and 4 Databricks Apps per industry. Every board opens in a Simplified view with Detailed view adding CI/CD, monitoring, operational stores, captions, capability tags, and descriptions; all boards work on Azure, AWS, and GCP (with ingestion tools changing by cloud), are translated into 16 languages including right-to-left Arabic and Hebrew, export to PowerPoint or PDF decks plus PNG, GIF, HTML, draw.io, Visio, SVG, Excalidraw, and YAML files, and can be rebuilt from a description via an AI Architecture Assistant that runs as a Databricks App with an accompanying MCP server exposing all 70 architectures. Boards filter products by region (dimming unavailable ones) and release stage (GA versus public preview or beta), drawing availability data from the public docs before each board update, though automated pipelines to refresh the board are planned rather than live; source code and a workspace installer are on GitHub. The item frames every industry board as only a starting point because companies have their own systems, constraints, history, sub-vertical differences, and changing vendor products, with out-of-date items reportable via a Feedback button.
items.title: Databricks publishes interactive reference architecture boards for 70 industries

items.summary: Anna Lenhart contends that rebuilding congressional capacity has been omitted from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries's stated priorities despite Congress being understaffed relative to its early-1990s peak. She attributes the shortfall partly to Speaker Newt Gingrich cutting committee staff by one-third in 1994 under the Contract with America, a reduction she says has not been reversed since. Lenhart draws on her experience as an aide from 2020 to 2023 to describe substantive tech policy work led by committee staff: the House Judiciary Antitrust Subcommittee's digital markets investigation (2019-2020), which received 1,287,997 documents and submissions from 60 experts plus interviews with more than 240 participants; and the American Data Privacy and Protection Act drafting (June 2022), which produced a 144-page final bill reported out of committee by a 53-2 vote. She notes that neither bill reached the president's desk for reasons other than lack of expertise, while chairmen allocated scarce staff to specific issues. Lenhart observes that subcommittees typically have three to four professional staff on the majority side and one to two on the minority side against an enormous jurisdictional scope. She proposes amending Rule X, clause 9 to increase overall professional staff and the share reserved for the minority party, with funding added through appropriations; she estimates rebuilding institutions like the FTC would require twice as many mid-career expert staff per subcommittee. Lenhart frames these figures and plans as claims rather than established outcomes: her staffing comparison is described as approximate ("just over half of its peak"), the 1994 cut is presented as one cause among others, and the Rule X proposal remains an untested recommendation pending election and appropriations approval.
items.title: Anna Lenhart argues congressional committee staffing is an underaddressed tech policy problem, citing a decline in staff to just over half of early-1990s peak levels.

items.summary: A pre-registered randomized experiment by Saharsh Agarwal of the Indian School of Business and Ananya Sen of Carnegie Mellon, conducted in early 2026 using a browser extension on 1,065 US adults on desktop Chrome, found that AI Overviews appearing organically reduced outbound clicks to websites from about 0.62 to 0.37 per search (a roughly 40% drop) and raised zero-click searches from 54% to 73%, with losses concentrated at the top of results; citations inside overviews generated only about 7% of those clicks, while ad clicks, Google's own-page traffic, total searches, dwell time, bounce rate, and self-reported search experience showed no change. The authors note the study cost around $30,000 to run plus months building the extension, and that it validates a 2025 Pew finding of lower click-through with AI summaries (8% versus 15%). Radsch argues these results undermine Google's unsubstantiated claim of fewer but better clicks, support remedies beyond publisher-by-publisher opt-outs given a collective-action problem, and point to regulatory action in the EU, UK CMA, Brazil CADE, and India as courts close the judicial route. The figures are reported measurements from the study rather than forecasts; no table is provided.
items.title: Independent study finds Google AI Overviews cut outbound clicks 40% with no user benefit

items.summary: Hugging Face reports that training a custom reinforcement-learning adapter on top of the frozen Qwen3.8-27B base model, using the agent harness itself as the trainer's environment and learning from its exact tokens via a proxy to vLLM, improves both accuracy and efficiency for that specific task-harness combination versus general-purpose models. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the Pi harness, freezing Qwen3.8-27B weights (which scored 39% pass@1 at an average of 2.9K tokens per task) and adding a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter raised performance to 55% pass@1 while cutting token usage to an average of 1.5K, largely because the model reasons less, calls fewer tools, and performs better on first attempts. The team trained one LoRA adapter per harness (Pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agent) with RL inside each harness using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, docker images pre-installed with those harnesses (Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7, Hermes Agent v0.22.6), and a Harbor/OpenEnv-based data pipeline combining SWE-smith, SWE-Gym/TaskTrove, and Tasksmith-generated tasks from merged pull requests; all artifacts are shared in Hugging Face collections (harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories). A task-eligibility screen kept only permissively licensed training-split tasks while dropping duplicates, benchmark evaluation sets, and repository-benchmark overlaps. Semantic checks required the reference solution to earn maximum reward, doing nothing to score clearly lower, no canary to exceed doing nothing, and a replay of the reference to give identical reward; 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed this screen (of which 442 scored tasks reduced Qwen3.8-27B's sometimes-solvable set to 171 qualified tasks). A separate difficulty check kept only tasks the base model solved on some but not all attempts; GRPO was avoided for always-or-never tasks because it yields no learning signal, and a final dataset of 278 directly-included tasks plus repaired-and-complexified rejected tasks came from this filtering. The reward function combined verifier correctness with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1). A learning-rate sweep on Termgrade environments settled on 2e-5 after finding that 1e-4 collapsed rollouts and longer runs showed instability, though the team noted training correctness stayed roughly flat during cumulative 598 steps of 78,114 samples (exactly 167M trained tokens) with no clear sign of saturation. Each adapter was trained on NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs; safeagents blocked a total of 647 tool calls across the three runs after checking 1.3M tool calls. The plain sum of the three adapters over-applied updates (making agents very short at 13 tool calls per task versus 49 for base, with Pi falling back to base level), while halving each update gave the best balance and formed the super-adapter from released checkpoints; under thinking-off conditions it improved on all six harness-benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 rising from 39.5% to 49.0%, solving 71 tasks newly versus losing 34, p < 0.001). The team cautions that the Terminal-Bench numbers for the super-adapter are slightly optimistic because the weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench with step-120 adapters and SWE-bench Pro played no part in that choice; full paired results are reported only in model cards, which they did not reproduce here. Transfer tests showed a Pi adapter matched OpenCode's specialist under OpenCode but kept about two-thirds of the gain under Hermes (differences within noise except perhaps Hermes), while out-of-distribution AutomationBench evaluation left adapters close to base with differences within noise; and community testing reported harness adapters working well on Qwen3.8 derivatives such as Swift-1.5, though they did not verify this claim themselves. The team identified a possible 'reasoning leakage' where the non-thinking model generates short text before tool calls that can resemble reasoning traces, but judged final results still valid under fixed token budgets and flagged hybrid thinking/non-thinking training as open follow-up work.
items.title: Hugging Face introduces RL-trained LoRA 'harness adapters' for Qwen3.8-27B

items.summary: The author explains that AI watermarking embeds a hidden signal in generated text so machines can detect machine-produced content and build filters against 'slop.' Anthropic reports its newest models plus some older ones now watermark output worldwide; Google has used a text watermark since 2024, and OpenAI announced one for ChatGPT and Codex in the EU. None of these companies lets the public verify text with their detectors—Google's synthid.com covers images, video, and audio but not AI text—and so only Anthropic-approved organizations can check Claude output yet; the author is applying for access. The article attributes two watermarking mechanisms to published work: a 2023 University of Maryland paper by John Kirchenbauer and colleagues ('A Watermark for Large Language Models') describes boosting probabilities for tokens on a per-token 'green list' determined by a secret key mixed with prior tokens, detectable statistically; Anthropic's Claude uses SynthID-Text from Google DeepMind (published in Nature 2024), which changes the randomness source used to pick among candidate words via coin flips keyed by word and context. A toy HTML page built for this article lets readers simulate detection: a five-digit key, token IDs as alphabetical positions, heads when a sum's last digit is 5-9, with 'Watermark detected' at 60%+ heads. The author notes the toy differs from real systems—real detectors use larger keys, hash functions instead of sums, and multiple weighted coin rounds trained on watermarked versus ordinary text—and that detection reliability scales with length: a short story's ~32 independent flips yield false positives roughly one in nine times. Because anyone holding the key can strip or forge watermarks, companies are withholding it from public use; the author flags this reasoning as their own understanding rather than confirmed fact.
items.title: Anthropic's Claude watermarks text, but public detection is withheld pending access approval

items.summary: Bloomberg reported, citing China's General Administration of Customs data, that Chinese solar cell exports jumped 21% year-over-year to 1.55 billion units in October—the second consecutive month of gains after four straight declines from May through August with a July trough. The rise follows Beijing removing the export tax rebate on photovoltaic products effective April 1, which had depressed volumes starting in May and was expected to slow exports going forward; China also plans to withdraw rebates on battery products as of January 1, 2027. A separate driver is a rush by buyers ahead of U.S. tariffs announced in August: the Trump Administration will impose minimum import prices for polysilicon and derivatives plus a 15% tariff effective December 4, framed as protecting national security. Separately, China's authorities are considering export controls or bans on about a dozen solar manufacturing technologies—such as perovskite, tandem, polysilicon, wafer, and crystalline-silicon cell production tech—as part of a broader effort to restrict up to 40 technologies across AI, biomedicine, and solar industries. The figures are Bloomberg's reported data; the tariff start date is December 4, 2026.
items.title: Chinese solar cell exports rose 21% in October on pre-tariff stockpiling

items.summary: The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a clean-and-dirty energy permitting reform co-authored by Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Sheldon Whitehouse (R-I), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), on a 62-to-33 vote; the House now considers it as supporters seek passage while bipartisan momentum remains ahead of Democratic control next year. The bill would streamline federal permitting for energy, infrastructure, transmission lines, data centers and fossil-fueled plants by changing environmental regulations and granting developers greater protections after greenlighting. Analysts expect it to accelerate renewable deployment and grid buildout, though the U.S. must still double or triple current transmission capacity to decarbonize the power grid by the mid-2030s per Princeton University's Repeat Project; opponents warn that changes to the Federal Power Act, Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act could let fossil fuel and data center projects proceed unchecked. Climate analysts are divided on emissions impact: Rhodium Group and Resources for the Future predict reduced greenhouse gas emissions, while other modelers project increased construction of fossil infrastructure would raise them; these projections remain uncertain. Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford called it a flawed bill that furthers fossil fuel buildout and strips power from communities and Tribes, urging House rejection, while Evergreen Action's Lena Moffitt acknowledged painful compromises but urged the House to pass it as part of building cheap clean energy at scale.
items.title: Senate passes bipartisan energy permitting bill by 62-33

items.summary: The Federal Reserve Board released, for release at 10:00 a.m. EST on Friday November 20, 2026, the results of its Senior Financial Officer Survey conducted in collaboration with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York between September 18 and September 28, 2026. The survey gathered information from senior financial officers at banks that held around three-fourths of total banking system reserve balances at the time, covering their strategies and practices for managing reserve balances, expectations about balance sheet size and deposit levels, money market activity, and views on weekend and holiday operations.
items.title: Federal Reserve Board releases Senior Financial Officer Survey results on bank reserve management

items.summary: Anthropic's initial public offering succeeded for shareholders, including its founders, but drew protests questioning whether the company can responsibly steward AI technology. The concerns are attributed to critics rather than established fact.
items.title: Protests over Anthropic's influence after first day of public trading

items.summary: Reuters reports that Anthropic announced on Friday its underwriters exercised a greenshoe option, raising the total proceeds from its initial public offering to roughly $93.5 billion. The figure is an announcement by Anthropic as relayed through Reuters; it reflects additional shares purchased via the option rather than new pricing.
items.title: Anthropic IPO proceeds rise to $93.5 billion after greenshoe exercise

items.summary: Anthropic's stock dropped more than 10% in premarket trading on Friday, then traded around $88.25, about 9% below Thursday's closing price of $97.17. The decline followed the company completing what Reuters reported as history's largest IPO, and occurred alongside a broader selloff hitting technology stocks worldwide. Analysts are questioning whether investors are reassessing high AI valuations.
items.title: Anthropic shares fell after record IPO amid AI selloff

items.summary: A pricing term sheet filed with the US SEC on Friday reported that Alphabet raised C$6 billion (about $4.19 billion) through a four-tranche Canadian bond offering priced November 19 and scheduled to settle November 24, per Reuters' account of the filing. The company expects about C$5.97 billion after underwriting discounts before expenses; the notes are senior unsecured debt rated Aa2 with stable outlook from Moody's and AA+ with stable outlook from S&P. RBC Dominion Securities, Scotia Capital and TD Securities were joint book-running managers, with CIBC World Markets as co-manager. The proceeds would go to general corporate purposes including possible repayment of outstanding debt. This is presented by the source as part of a broader shift toward debt markets for AI infrastructure; that framing is attributed to the reporting rather than established fact. For context, Meta announced plans in October for its largest-ever equity offerings around $97.5 billion (including about $37.5 billion stock sales) plus up to $60 billion via an at-the-market program, and Alphabet had raised $84.75 billion in equity by June; the source also noted Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in Q3 versus analysts' expectation of near breakeven.
items.title: Alphabet raises C$6 billion in four-tranche Canadian bond offering

items.summary: A Bloomberg report citing an Apple job listing says the company is building an AI system that could go beyond answering questions by operating on its own. The reported capabilities include browsing websites, running apps, executing commands, writing code, and fixing errors in it, plus breaking large tasks into smaller pieces handled by separate agents so users may need to open fewer apps. Apple reportedly aims to introduce the technology by late 2027, though development is described as early and no launch date is set; this timeline is a report-based claim rather than an official commitment. New CEO John Ternus is said to be pushing for faster progress on AI plans. The agent would compete with OpenAI, Google, Meta and Anthropic, which reportedly already have such tools in development. Separately reported, Apple intends greater Siri integration with third-party apps under iOS 27.3, potentially easing tasks like booking cabs and restaurants; macOS 27.3 is also said to involve a lengthy process for granting third-party AI computer-control permission, raising competition concerns. Because the agent would need access to apps, files and other services, Apple reportedly emphasizes privacy and security through permissions, limited access and transparency.
items.title: Apple reportedly developing autonomous AI agent to operate apps and websites, targeting a 2027 launch

items.summary: At the November 20, 2026 opening remarks for the finals of the annual College Fed Challenge at the Federal Reserve Board in Washington, D.C., Chairman John C. Williams—referred to as 'Waller' in the document's title—framed the student competition as a mirror of FOMC deliberations. The event, begun 23 years earlier under Alan Greenspan and running since 2003, drew a record 141 participating schools from 34 states; seven teams representing UCLA, the University of Chicago, Cleveland State University, Harvard College, the University of Maryland, College Park, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University advanced to compete on December 8-9. The Chair noted that FOMC members will present their economic-outlook views publicly on December 8 and their policy-stance views on December 9 after internal discussion aimed at consensus in a postmeeting statement. He emphasized clear communication as essential because monetary policy works partly by shaping public expectations, described the dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment, traced FOMC tool evolution from setting a federal funds rate target to adding unconventional tools, and thanked judges including Sriya Anbil, Karen Pence, Brian Doyle, Sam Schulhofer-Wohl (adviser to Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan), faculty advisers, and economic education staff. The remarks carry the disclaimer that views are personal and not necessarily those of Board or FOMC colleagues.
items.title: Fed Chair Waller opens 2026 College Fed Challenge Finals

items.summary: Washington's efforts, since 2022, to restrict Chinese access to advanced semiconductors were catalyzed by an espionage scandal that led to the ousting of Nvidia's CEO. California officials are investigating whether Nvidia misled investors about its links to Beijing, while federal lawmakers released files showing the US approved sales of nearly 880,000 chips to China, including to firms seen as fronts for the Chinese military. Caixin reported China's tech giants were reeling from the prospect of new semiconductor restrictions.
items.title: US scrutiny intensifies on chip sales to China after Nvidia scandal

items.summary: The VoxDev newsletter for 20/11/2026 previews a week of featured research. David Lagakos, with Daniel Björkegren and Mitchell VanVuren, present one of the first macroeconomic frameworks for AI's impact on developing-world growth, arguing that a country's AI future may be decided as much in high-income countries as at home; this is presented as an upcoming discussion rather than established findings. Oeindrila Dube and Michael Callen discuss conflict and fragility from their IGC–BREAD PhD lecture, noting armed conflict is now more widespread than at any point since records began and increasingly concentrated where extreme poverty persists. Craig McIntosh explains how to maximise value from randomised controlled trials by running them alongside programme expansion, using A/B tests of improvements, and agreeing roles, costs, and outcomes with an independent research team from the start; this is guidance rather than reported results. Siddharth George and Martin Mattsson evaluate India's village secretary pay raise, finding that doubling their salaries made secretaries more likely to stay but did not improve performance or reduce corruption. Leonardo Flori and Nicola Limodio report that across 339 remittance corridors worldwide, fees rise when the recipient country's currency becomes more volatile, with this currency risk adding about as much to transfer price as operators' markups, concluding competition alone cannot lower these costs. The roundup also lists Esteban Ortiz-Ospina on women now being globally more likely than men to enrol in higher education, and Eeshani Kandpal on the extent India has reduced poverty; both are listed without reported findings.
items.title: VoxDev roundup of development economics research from 20 November 2026

items.summary: Google began rolling out a 'computer use' feature in its Gemini app for Mac, letting users describe tasks while Gemini performs clicking, typing, menu and form actions across local files, desktop apps and the web. The capability runs in a separate background window with live previews so the user's display remains free, and it requires Google AI Plus, Pro or Ultra subscriptions; availability is limited to English in the U.S., per Bloomberg. Users can choose which apps Gemini may open, follow each step, halt tasks at any time, or approve important actions first. OpenAI ChatGPT and Meta Muse already offer comparable Mac automation for local files and programs, while Google provided no timeline for other countries or operating systems, per TechCrunch.
items.title: Google rolls out computer use for Gemini on Mac

items.summary: Cathie Wood's ARK Invest purchased roughly $90.8 million of Anthropic stock, about 935,000 shares total, spread across six of its funds on the company's Nasdaq trading debut, according to CNBC and CoinDesk citing an emailed trading update. The ARK Innovation ETF held 556,777 of those shares; Anthropic now represents 0.3% of that fund's $6.1 billion in assets, ranking outside its top 10 holdings behind Tesla and SpaceX, which together exceed 21%. This was a new purchase layered onto ARK's existing pre-IPO position held through the ARK Venture Fund. Wood typically builds favored positions gradually over extended periods; the Innovation ETF is down more than 10% this year versus the S&P 500's gain of 4.8%. Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, selling 980 million Class A shares for an offering totaling $81 billion, which topped SpaceX's prior $75 billion raise before underwriter overage; the company itself receives no proceeds from certain stockholders' portion and granted underwriters a 30-day option on up to 147 million additional shares. On its debut day Anthropic opened at $111.50, closed at $97.17 (down 13% intraday), finishing 17% above the IPO price; it traded lower in Friday premarket.
items.title: ARK Invest bought Anthropic shares across six funds on IPO debut

items.summary: The Three Choirs vineyard near Newent, Gloucestershire, released a First Release dry white wine of 5,000 bottles made from solaris, bacchus, siegerrebe and madeleine angevine grapes. The winery calls the release its 'Gloucestershire nouveau,' a tongue-in-cheek nod to France's Beaujolais nouveau tradition; it is not an established equivalent of that practice but a marketing comparison. This year's harvest was the earliest in the vineyard's 50 years, with picking beginning on 20 August and ending on 9 October across its 30 hectares (74 acres), yielding about 200 tonnes of grapes; this beats the previous record set in 2025. Three Choirs' winemaking director Martin Fowke attributed the early timing to warm temperatures, higher sugar levels and lower acidity, saying these conditions allowed a product not possible in Britain 30 years ago. He also said that three consecutive good harvest years would be unusual rather than common. The vineyard has produced wine since vines were first planted on the site of a fruit farm in 1973 and bottled young wine every November since the 1980s, when harvesting began around mid-September; it now produces for about 40 other producers including Llanerch west of Cardiff. The article notes that Britain's vineyard area has quadrupled since the turn of the century according to Knight Frank and that English and Welsh producers had their second-largest harvest in 2025, producing the equivalent of 16.5m bottles or 124,377 hectolitres per WineGB; it also states that more than 1,100 vineyards are registered in Britain. The UK remains a small global wine producer by volume but is described as the fastest-growing region according to Knight Frank. Fowke said pruning for the 2027 season had already begun and cautioned against expecting further warming.
items.title: Three Choirs vineyard releases its 2026 'Gloucestershire nouveau' white wine after an early harvest

items.summary: Britannia Jinky Jersey, parent company of Pontins, was fined £1m and pleaded guilty to breaching the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 after a ceiling collapse killed Wendy Jones, 68. The Brean Sands Fun Factory incident in February 2019 injured eighteen people; ventilation ducting and a 40-metre section of ceiling fell during bingo while Jones sat on her mobility scooter with about 100 others. She died six months later after a postmortem linked the injuries to her death. An investigation by Avon and Somerset police, Somerset council and the Health and Safety Executive found ventilation ducting had been poorly installed decades earlier but that soundproofing work in 2015 was the immediate cause: contractor Stephen Bennison stacked heavy insulation slabs on the ducting without assessing whether it could bear the weight. The material appeared to be leftover stock with no practical purpose, and neither Britannia Jinky Jersey nor Bennison assessed its load-bearing capacity. CPS specialist prosecutor Rachael Taylor said Jones's death was avoidable; she is quoted as saying a family holiday ended in tragedy because basic safety responsibilities were not met (16 words).
items.title: Pontins owner fined £1m over death at Somerset holiday park

items.summary: Global stock markets slumped as Anthropic's debut failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies, following Thursday losses where the main indices fell by over 2%. The IPO placed Anthropic as the biggest ever, with 980m shares sold raising $81bn and demand reportedly about six times what was offered. Senior Democrats have suggested tech firms could face regulatory action over advanced-AI dangers and AI-IPO volatility, though this is a proposal rather than an established outcome. The seven co-founders are reported to be worth $180bn combined.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO fails to halt global AI stock slide

items.summary: Christine Lagarde stepped down as European Central Bank president on 29 October, reigniting speculation about a possible bid to become France's first female president in an election five months away. She remains bound by political neutrality until February 2027 and has repeatedly declined to confirm candidacy, telling La Croix that running at age 70 would not be advisable while expressing interest only in matters beyond monetary policy. Analysts caution her appeal is limited: Bruno Cautrès of Sciences Po says her polling reflects the right's lack of direction rather than genuine enthusiasm, noting she could resonate with educated centrist and conservative voters but risks being seen as an out-of-touch technocrat. Bernard Dolez said a Lagarde candidacy would not take votes from Mélenchon or Le Pen but might attract supporters of Gabriel Attal and Édouard Philippe. A Politico survey on 11 November put her at 13.5% versus 14% for Philippe, while an Ifop-Fiducial poll dated 18 November showed Marine Le Pen around 32-34% and Jean-Luc Mélenchon at 17-19.5%. The article offers no figures to compare across named candidates; the reported numbers are separate polls measuring different things for different people, so a chart is not warranted.
items.title: Speculation grows over whether ECB President Lagarde could run for France's presidency

items.summary: TikTok announced on Friday that it began rolling out an opt-in feature called 'Likeness Detection' to help public figures, including politicians, government members and political party accounts, find and flag AI-generated content using their likeness without consent. Eligible users verify ID through a trusted third-party partner before signing up; they are then notified of suspected uses and can report flagged content directly to TikTok's safety teams for review. The launch coincides with Europe facing AI-driven disinformation ahead of nine more European elections within 12 months, though the article frames this timing as context rather than establishing causation. On 2 August the EU began rolling out transparency rules under the AI Act, including a requirement that deepfakes and other AI-generated content be labelled; TikTok has also complied by requiring creators to label realistic AI images, audio and video. A separate free tool called 'Identify AI-Generated Content' lets anyone upload an image or video to check whether it was generated or edited with TikTok's own tools including ByteDance apps CapCut, Dreamina, Hypic and Pippit; supported formats include JPEG, PNG and MP4, with a file size limit of 20 megabytes per image or 100 megabytes for each video or audio. The tool checks metadata credentials added by TikTok and ByteDance apps plus invisible watermarks embedded directly into content that are harder to remove. TikTok states it deletes all uploaded content immediately after checking and never uses uploads to train AI models, but warns the tool only detects content created with its own or ByteDance app tools and is not a foolproof way to spot AI-generated material.
items.title: TikTok rolls out Likeness Detection and Identify AI-Generated Content tools

items.summary: Anthropic raised US$81 billion in its initial public offering on Nasdaq, surpassing SpaceX's prior all-time IPO record of US$75 billion. Its share price rose from an opening offer around US$83 to a debut high of US$111 before closing at US$97.17, up 17% and valuing the company at about US$1.76 trillion versus SpaceX's roughly US$2.1 trillion on its first day; briefly it nudged past US$2 trillion as investors took profits. The listing occurred amid sector caution over AI spending and following Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, yet the author cautions that enthusiasm for Anthropic should not be read as a vote of confidence in the broader AI industry. Demand was strong: Bloomberg reported the offering about six times oversubscribed while only around 15% of shares went to retail investors. Revenue underpinned demand with an October annualised run rate of US$81 billion, though third-quarter revenue growth slowed from 144% in Q2 to 47%, and token prices have fallen amid cheaper models; the company also warned that some customers depend on external financing. Going public exposes Anthropic to greater scrutiny over governance, safety, privacy and social responsibility, with CEO Dario Amodei acknowledging real risks while expressing faith in balancing them commercially. OpenAI has now deferred its own listing until 2027 citing safety concerns, but gains a financial yardstick from Anthropic at the cost of facing intensified public attention amid protests calling for regulation or an AI pause.
items.title: Anthropic's record $81 billion Nasdaq listing and what it signals for AI

items.summary: Brittany Masalosalo, HP's chief public policy officer, told CGTN that technology and innovation from China produce worldwide benefits. She stated that HP remains keen on partnerships with China's tech ecosystem and cited many reasons to be optimistic about the relationship.
items.title: HP public policy officer argues for continued partnership with China's tech sector

items.summary: China hosted its third APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, opening November 18 with the CEO Summit and culminating on November 19 in Xi Jinping's meeting with Putin and Trump. In keynotes delivered before that summit, Xi posed three questions about global direction and urged leaders to abandon a cold-war mentality while avoiding decoupling of supply chains; he stressed that prosperity requires security and stability and called for peace, openness, cooperation and innovation as foundations for the region. The article notes China is not directly involved in the conflicts cited (Iran, Ukraine, Middle East tensions) but frames Xi's calls—including one for a nuclear-free world—as carrying particular weight because of this distance; these are the author's characterizations rather than established facts. It reports that Xi, Putin and Trump adopted a joint declaration covering UN reform, stable energy supplies, state sovereignty and officials' immunity, while asserting as opinion that declarations alone will not produce fundamental change and that real change requires action. The piece presents China's economic claims—having eradicated absolute poverty by 2020 under its national standard, holding the world's second-largest economy, entering its 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030) focused on innovation-driven growth and a greener economy, and recording 4.6% growth in the first three quarters of 2026—as stated figures without independent verification; these are attributed to China's own reporting rather than confirmed by an external source. The article concludes as opinion that APEC should move beyond consensus toward practical commitments, leaving leaders with both a shared understanding and actionable pledges.
items.title: Xi's APEC keynote framed China as a peace-builder ahead of his three-way summit

items.summary: NASA confirmed on Thursday that Voyager 1 became the most distant human-made object by traveling beyond a light-day—about 26 billion kilometers—from Earth after 49 years, 2 months and 11 days of flight. The milestone was verified when a radio signal sent from interstellar space reached Madrid through NASA's Deep Space Network; because the signal takes roughly a day to arrive, the crossing occurred Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT). Engineer Nshan Kazaryan announced it at JPL in California, and science lead Nicola Fox called it an "amazing day." The probe entered interstellar space in 2012 after passing Jupiter and Saturn, flies toward the star Gliese 445 roughly 17 light-years away (projected to pass within about 1.7 light-years in around 40,000 years), travels at nearly 61,000 kilometers per hour, and is running low on power amid technical anomalies—though Fox said the mission "is never going to end." Twin Voyager 2 entered interstellar space in 2018. For context, a light-year spans about 9.5 trillion kilometers; one light-day is roughly 1/365 of that distance.
items.title: NASA confirms Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth, first human-made object to do so

items.summary: The UN released its biennial 2026 E-Government Survey, reporting that the Republic of Korea leads a global ranking of 193 member states plus Palestine on scope and quality of online services, telecommunications infrastructure and human capital. Denmark, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iceland, Britain, Estonia, Finland and Australia round out the top ten; the very high EGDI class expanded from 18 to 21 countries with Ireland, Kazakhstan and Poland joining for the first time and the United States returning. The global average EGDI rose 4.6%, from 0.6382 in 2024 to 0.6675 in 2026; among the 35 countries that changed groups, 28 moved up and seven down, while ten remain low-rated. All regions improved, with Oceania gaining most at 15.5% and Africa second at 10.5%, yet about 87% of Africa's population lives below the global average and roughly 1.95 billion people (about a quarter of the world) live in countries under that average, up from 2024 by 53.3 million. At the local level, very high LOSI cities rose from 42 to 68 across 194 assessed; Dubai, Madrid, Manama, Riyadh, Sao Paulo and Vienna scored highest. The survey frames an emerging shift toward AI-enabled or agentic public administration while stressing that officials must retain decision responsibility through trusted data, cybersecurity, human oversight and auditable safeguards, lest inequalities deepen into a new AI divide. UN Assistant Secretary-General Navid Hanif said the fundamental principle is trust, quoting: "Technology can enable transformation. Only transparent, accountable and responsive institutions can earn public trust." He added that digitalization must accelerate while reaching local communities and warned of an emerging development divide.
items.title: UN 2026 E-Government Survey: South Korea tops ranking as digital divide widens

items.summary: The Youth Strike coalition describes coordinated demonstrations in more than 20 European countries as Europe's biggest youth protest of recent years. Organisers from more than 50 groups staged rallies on Friday under the slogan "fight for our future" or "fight for our future, not their wars," with planned participation across roughly 400 cities. The coalition set five broad demands: an end to militarisation and conscription; structural investment in education and welfare; solidarity with Palestine; climate and social justice; and a radical transformation of the system. Alessandro di Miceli, an Italian organiser, characterised the protests as claiming young people's right to a dignified future while noting that specific demands varied by country but remained interconnected. Leonor Chicó, from Portugal, framed participation as self-organising because governments do not prioritise this generation's needs. Shabbir Lakha of Stop The War called it a step toward an international movement uniting young people, students and workers around common demands. The Friday rallies followed weeks of demonstrations across several countries originating in French school protests; France saw gilets jaunes participation, Germany drew about 1,000 Berlin students concerned about compulsory military service returning, Italy held tens of thousands protesting amid a CGIL general strike against Giorgia Meloni's government, and London featured youth-led marches. The report attributes the framing as Europe's biggest protest to Youth Strike itself; it is not independently verified.
items.title: Youth Strike coalition coordinates youth protests across Europe over cost of living, housing, education and militarisation

items.summary: President Trump was set to hold a 12 p.m. ET White House press conference following his return from a four-day Asia trip that included a rare summit of himself with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a lakeside resort in Shenzhen, where the three nuclear-armed leaders discussed nuclear proliferation, Iran, and global relations. Trump said he would address both the meetings and trade agreements reached earlier during a Philippine summit; he did not formally take questions while in China but Putin held one before leaving. Suzanne Maloney of Brookings characterized the trip as an opportunity for Trump to project great-power amity after a difficult election outcome rather than secure substantive concessions, noting that Xi sought to showcase global leadership and Putin aimed to reestablish Russia's standing on par with China and the U.S. The article attributed the absence of major deliverables partly to Maloney's claim that both leaders judged Trump's political command as waning amid domestic midterm losses and were watching for successors.
items.title: Trump scheduled a noon White House press conference after a three-way Xi-Putin meeting in Shenzhen

items.summary: Floating offshore wind, a nascent technology for harvesting renewable energy in deep waters where fixed-bottom turbines are impractical, remains pre-commercial with roughly 300 MW of global pilot capacity versus nearly 100 GW worldwide from fixed wind. Hywind Tampen in Norway is the largest installation at 94.6 MW across 11 floating turbines. Louise Efthimiou of World Forum Offshore Wind calls it a strong decarbonization contender for markets constrained by water depth, while Amisha Patel of the Global Offshore Wind Alliance notes momentum but stresses that policy drivers are needed to reach scalable buildout after economic headwinds slowed progress from 2020's projection of up to 16.5 GW installed by 2030. Developers cite high costs and immature supply chains as specific obstacles, with Enrico Giglio, Bruno Paduano, Riccardo Longo, and researchers at Polytechnic University of Torino arguing that standardization could cut costs but must be paired with bankable projects, suitable ports, grid availability, and long-term investor visibility; a 2025 paper adds gigawatt-scale farms will lower costs yet demand major investment in ports, vessels, cables, and industrialization. Government port investments are underway in France (260 million Euros/$286 million across five ports), the U.K., and California's state funds, while China positions itself as a potential leader and Japan targets 15 GW by 2040. Recent milestones include Japan's first commercial farm at 16.8 MW launched in January 2026, Ocean Winds' 30 MW French operation from May, and China aiming to finish a 1 GW farm by 2027, offset by setbacks such as Italy's stalled funding bid in 2025, Australia scrapping a planned 2 GW farm that year, South Korea losing a 750 MW project in 2026, and a U.K. cancellation over blocked Mingyang turbines. Amy Robertson of the Technical University of Denmark attributes future cost declines to economies of scale, system-level costs, and learning effects; Louise Efthimiou identifies reaching a 250 MW-plus farm by 2030 as a key stepping stone for further growth. Environmental impacts are largely shared with fixed-bottom wind—increased ship traffic, noise pollution, wildlife collisions—but floating systems may avoid seabed disturbance during construction while introducing entanglement risks from mooring and inter-array cables; Clémentine Mitoyen of the Mediterranean research team flagged habitat overlap with 135 vulnerable species, Douglas Nowacek of Duke University judged primary and secondary cable-entanglement risk minimal but unproven, and Efthimiou called for more coordinated long-term impact study. Daniel Merino of COWI cautioned that gigawatt-scale projects require investment conditions not yet present, predicting a slow pace while cheaper fixed-bottom wind remains the focus.
items.title: Floating wind is advancing toward commercialization amid cost and supply-chain barriers

items.summary: Ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, Formula One team principals reported that stakeholders had agreed in principle to replace current V6 hybrid power units with louder V8s starting in 2030. McLaren's Zak Brown described it as remaining administrative work rather than a completed deal, while Alpine's Flavio Briatore said "the agreement" was basically reached but not signed; he argued the move suits spectators and favored simplicity over complexity. Dan Towriss of Cadillac expressed satisfaction with developments, noting his team would keep using Ferrari engines until the end of 2029 before introducing a Cadillac V8 from 2030. FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem had separately signalled that naturally aspirated V8s would return in 2030, recalling their prior use as Formula One's power unit between 2006 and 2013.
items.title: F1 stakeholders agree in principle on a switch to V8 engines from 2030

items.summary: Poland reported that three objects violated its airspace early Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying the incident did not appear accidental while Western military exercises were underway. Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said a Kh-101 cruise missile hit Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km from Ukraine's border at around 06:30 local time, with two other objects crashing near Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz. Nobody was hurt and no damage reported, though Warsaw called the incursion a "provocation" from Moscow; Russia made no comment. The strikes coincided with the Koalicja 2026 exercise in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries of the West's Coalition of the Willing group. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned the airspace violations and said jets were scrambled, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Prime Minister Andy Burnham also commented on the incident. The event followed a Berlin summit where 40 countries pledged continued support for Ukraine; separately at least eight people died in Kyiv when Russian missiles hit three bridges across the Dnipro River and a station in Lviv. Poland has previously suffered missile strikes, including one in July that created a crater and two farmers killed by a missile in November 2022 believed to be a Ukrainian air-defence response; Moldova also reported airspace violations on Friday amid Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
items.title: Russian missile strikes Poland during Western military exercise, Tusk calls it a provocation

items.summary: The Taliban accuse Pakistan of funding and arming opposition groups, with Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi alleging a "project to destabilize Afghanistan" and claiming thousands of armed individuals have gathered along the Durand Line. Spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid alleged that anti-Taliban fighters in Badakhshan crossed from Chitral after being brought in by Pakistani military personnel. Pakistan's Ministry of Information dismissed these claims as propaganda, while opposition groups insist their resistance is indigenous and unsupported externally. Analysts remain divided: Afrasiab Khattak asserts support for Taliban opponents "is real," Qandil Abbas contends only political rather than military backing occurs, and Ali Ahmad Jalali suggests Islamabad may use such support as leverage. Pakistan counters by accusing the Taliban of enabling TTP and Baloch Liberation Army attacks from Afghan territory, a demand Jalali argues exceeds what Kabul can provide given ideological ties between the groups. Analysts also cite the Taliban's closer ties with India as a concern for Islamabad, though Jalali maintains Pakistan does not seek to overthrow the Taliban but rather pressures them toward cooperation; Aziz Barez warns opposition groups may distrust Pakistani support as potentially temporary.
items.title: Pakistan denies backing anti-Taliban Afghan groups amid border tensions

items.summary: The article describes RunPee, a free application created by software developer Dan Gardner to identify optimal moments during films for taking a bathroom break. The motivation stems from the growing length of movies and the disappearance of intermissions; two recent box-office hits reportedly run close to three hours each, with upcoming releases cited at 2.5 hours and 2 hours 45 minutes. RunPee maintains a catalog of more than 2,300 films used by roughly 250,000 moviegoers annually according to the website's own figures. The app displays a green thumbs-up for ideal breaks or a red thumbs-down indicating departure only in an emergency, vibrates about 30 seconds before each designated break, and provides summaries of on-screen content during absences. Gardner and a small team reportedly time films, choosing montages or scenes already shown in trailers; the article attributes this selection method to volunteer Rob Williams's explanation given to The Guardian. During Barbenheimer in summer 2023, more than 100,000 downloads are reported over those days according to Gardner. RunPee also alerts users to post-credits scenes and warns of distressing content such as violence, sex, torture and animal cruelty; the article notes a parallel website called Does the Dog Die offers similar warnings about whether dogs die in films. The piece presents these details as reporting rather than established fact, with several figures drawn from RunPee's own claims or attributed to specific sources.
items.title: RunPee, an app that signals when moviegoers can leave for a bathroom break

items.summary: A European Union debate programme, prepared by Oihana Almandoz, Perrine Desplats and Isabelle Romero, is set to host MEPs from both sides of Spain's political spectrum ahead of a parliamentary election scheduled for November 29. The item frames the vote as potentially ending the Socialist-led government under Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, possibly forming a right-to-far-right coalition in one of the EU's largest member states and concluding his third term; these are presented as possibilities rather than outcomes. It attributes to opponents' framing claims that Sanchez may face political consequences for two train crashes and a migrant crisis in Ceuta, and characterizes corruption allegations against his inner circle as making him an 'embarrassing European symbol,' while noting the European left's limited number of governing governments across the bloc.
items.title: Spain's parliamentary election on November 29

items.summary: At a Friday Brussels summit, EU officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced agreements on food exports, linking emissions-trading systems, and a youth experience scheme. The youth scheme would let 100,000 people under 30 from each side reside up to three years in the other's territory for work, study or travel without existing visa requirements; Burnham framed it as improving young people's life chances after Brexit "took opportunities" from them. Under the food deal both sides would scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products, with Britain aligning more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules. The emissions agreement links their trading systems to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes; von der Leyen said it could cut emissions and generate investment in cleaner industries. No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students, which the bloc treated as a deal-breaker by pressing for UK fees reduced to British levels, though Burnham expected further talks within about a month. AFP reports London estimates the deal could boost the economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation. The leaders also agreed to establish structured dialogue on migration covering engagement with third countries and returns, plus formal talks on economic security and cooperation on export controls and supply chains. Burnham called the agreements "probably the limit" achievable in this Parliament given implementation needs; von der Leyen described it as a turning point while Costa joked that despite driving on opposite sides of the road they are heading for the same direction. Separately, YouGov polling since mid-2022 shows a majority saying Britain was wrong to leave, with "Bregret" reaching 60% in September.
items.title: EU and UK agree trade, youth mobility deals at Brussels summit

items.summary: Bank of Maharashtra's Managing Director and CEO Nidhu Saxena said at the CII-DFS Financing Summit that an additional $100-175 million Medium-Term Note (MTN) issuance is being considered, with proceeds to fund credit growth over five years. The bank has not yet decided; Saxena cited awareness of prevailing interest rates and US Treasury yield movements as factors affecting commercial viability, noting the transaction would be explored before December 31 under the RBI's swap window if pursued. He contrasted this with a completed $500 million dollar bond issue that was subscribed nearly three times its target amount. Separately, Saxena discussed expanding the bank's GIFT International Banking Unit (IBU), which reached a $2 billion business book within a year and raised FCNR(B) deposits in a one-off opportunity he described as significant for leverage.
items.title: Bank of Maharashtra considering $100-175 million MTN issuance under RBI swap window

items.summary: After Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO opened at $111.50 per share, the stock became one of the highest-traded titles on platforms allowing Indians to trade global equities. Vested reported that Anthropic represented about 11 percent of all traded value and 9 percent of trades by volume, with an average buy order around $1,100; roughly 20 percent of active traders bought it, and about 84 percent of its trades occurred within two hours of listing. Viram Shah, Vested's founder and CEO, attributed the interest to direct exposure to AI models rather than only semiconductor or infrastructure names. Indmoney reported that Anthropic bids were twice its platform average and accounted for 40 percent of order volume on Thursday; it did not disclose absolute investment values. Neither company disclosed total customer investments in Anthropic—Vested's last-reported assets stood at ₹15,000 crore across about 5 lakh accounts with 80 percent held in US public markets, while Indmoney reported around $3.5 billion under management. Shares closed their first session at $97.17, up 17.07 percent from the listing price. Naresh Biyani of Capwise Financial Service cautioned that early moves reflect trading flows rather than fundamentals, with a real test pending quarterly results and lock-in expiry; these are claims without supporting evidence in the item.
items.title: Anthropic among most-traded stocks by Indian retail investors after its IPO listing

items.summary: Anthropic, creator of Claude AI and co-founded in 2021 by Dario Amodei after he left OpenAI, debuted on Nasdaq on November 19, 2026. Its IPO price was $83; the share rose to $111.50 intraday before closing at $97.17, up 17.07%, then slipped to $92.58 in after-hours trading per Nasdaq data. Per a Reuters report, options on Anthropic shares may begin trading November 23, and reports suggest investors could also gain access to 2x ETFs that magnify both gains and losses. The article notes these instruments carry risks including total loss of the investment; leveraged ETFs reset daily and can lose value quickly, so it advises research and consultation with a licensed financial professional before large or risky decisions. All figures are attributed: IPO price ($83), intraday high ($111.50), closing price ($97.17), after-hours close ($92.58), 17.07% gain, November 19 debut date, and the Reuters-sourced November 23 options start are reported claims rather than confirmed outcomes.
items.title: Options trading for Anthropic shares may begin November 23, per Reuters.

items.summary: Anthropic, maker of AI chatbot Claude, listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under ticker ANT, with shares closing 17.07% higher at $97.17 after opening more than 30% above the initial public offering price. The company raised $81.31 billion through its IPO, which it describes as a record for largest IPO at initial pricing and surpassing SpaceX's earlier $75 billion offering; this is presented by the source as an established fact rather than independently verified. The deal comprised 980 million Class A common shares, of which Anthropic sold 956.35 million while existing shareholders offered 23.65 million, with no proceeds going to those selling shareholders. The IPO is expected to value the company at more than $1 trillion, though this valuation figure is a forecast rather than an outcome. Indian investors who missed the offering can buy shares only at prevailing market prices through overseas brokerage accounts under the Reserve Bank of India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), which permits remittances up to $250,000 per financial year for permitted transactions including foreign stocks; platforms such as Zerodha, Groww and HDFC Securities are named as offering access. The source notes that GIFT City-based platforms may also provide a route depending on their products and regulatory arrangements, but this is offered conditionally rather than confirmed.
items.title: Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO and how Indian investors can access its shares

items.summary: Anthropic completed what was described as the largest public stock offering ever, raising $81.31 billion and surpassing SpaceX's prior haul of $75 billion; shares opened at $111.50, about 34% above the $83 IPO price, before closing up 17.07% at $97.17 for a valuation that briefly crossed $2 trillion and settled around $1.75 trillion (Reuters cited a fully diluted figure of roughly $1.7 trillion against market capitalisation near $1.2 trillion). The listing was framed as the first public-market access to a pure-play AI developer rather than chip, infrastructure or data-centre suppliers, with StoneX's Fiona Cincotta calling it "the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," and analysts noting its potential role as an industry valuation benchmark ahead of OpenAI's possible 2026 listing. Despite strong demand—orders reportedly exceeding supply by more than six times—the debut did not lift sentiment, with US stocks under pressure on Thursday and Anthropic shares falling about 6% in premarket Friday trading to $91.24; Mudrex's Prateek Gupta said the broader market was already strained as investors reassess AI valuations, while Passion Capital's Eileen Burbidge suggested a bubble slowdown but not an imminent burst. Concerns cited include revenue concentration (roughly a quarter from Google and Amazon, two-thirds from the US), heavy spending on chips, data centres and talent with some employees reportedly earning over $100 million annually, circular financing arrangements, and safety risks that Anthropic's SEC filing addressed across 93 pages; CEO Dario Amodei told Jamie Dimon his principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth."
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO debut did not lift broader tech sentiment

items.summary: Leaker Sonny Dickson shared dummy-model images of Apple's planned iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 on X. The dummies indicate the iPhone Air 2 would add a second rear camera lens alongside its current single 48MP Fusion sensor, with lenses arranged horizontally toward the left side of the camera plateau while microphone and flash sit to the right; Dickson frames this as another added rear camera, though earlier reporting from The Information suggested the addition is an ultra-wide rather than telephoto lens. In contrast, the iPhone 18 dummy shows two rear cameras matching the current iPhone 17's configuration. Dummy models are built from leaked supply-chain design specifications and dimensions to help manufacturers develop cases before launch; they reflect reported specs rather than confirmed hardware. The iPhone Air 2 is also rumored to gain an A20 Pro chipset, larger battery, vapor chamber cooling, C2 modem, and N2 wireless chip, while the standard iPhone 18 may use the A20 with a smaller Dynamic Island and C2 modem. All three devices are expected to launch in March 2027 alongside the entry-level iPhone 18e.
items.title: Dummy models suggest dual rear cameras on future iPhone Air, unchanged design for standard iPhone 18

items.summary: Anthropic shares fell to $88.87, roughly 9% below Thursday's debut close, yielding a fully diluted valuation of about $1.6 trillion and a market capitalization of $1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding. The decline added to broader weakness in the sector: Wall Street indexes closed sharply lower on Thursday with Friday futures pointing further down, while Nvidia and Meta fell more than 2% each premarket, Amazon and Microsoft dropped more than 1%, and AMD, Sandisk, and Intel slid 7%, 7%, and more than 5% respectively. Kaush Amin of US Bank Asset Management advised patience, noting the valuation assumes years of rapid growth. Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could buy up to 30% of Anthropic's shares by year-end as a potential support source later in the year, though near-term volatility may persist while investors assess whether roughly 40 times sales over the past 12 months can hold. Attention now turns to OpenAI, which has indicated it may go public next year.
items.title: Anthropic's post-debut slide deepens gloom over AI trade

items.summary: Abhinav, a man from Ghazipur district in Uttar Pradesh who worked at a private company in Chennai and reportedly followed the social media influencer Neha Bisht on Instagram, allegedly entered her residence in Madhu Vihar, Delhi's Madhur Vihar area on November 7 while intoxicated to propose marriage. After she was unaware of his identity and had recently posted about her engagement and upcoming wedding, members of her family and neighbours assaulted him; police found him with serious injuries to his back and right foot when they arrived at the residence. He died during treatment at Rajiv Gandhi Hospital on November 15. Police registered a case of culpable homicide and arrested Neha's father, Virender Bisht, along with a neighbour, while CCTV footage from the area is being examined to identify other suspects.
items.title: Man dies after allegedly being beaten for proposing to Delhi influencer Neha Bisht

items.summary: The Reserve Bank of India issued FAQs on Friday to clarify foreign exchange reporting requirements for services imports and exports. The clarification states that the ₹10 lakh reporting threshold applies separately to each inward remittance rather than cumulatively across payments received by a service exporter. Non-individual exporters receiving remittances above the limit must submit an Export Declaration Form (EDF) before funds are credited, while resident individuals were exempted from declaration requirements in November under a monetary threshold introduced earlier that month. The RBI also clarified that authorised banks may grant extensions for export declarations when they find exporters' reasons justified, and that banks must publish trade-related policies and key operating procedures on their official websites. The revised framework was originally notified in January with reporting effective Oct 1, and the central bank said it aims to align India's foreign exchange regulations with international trade practices while improving ease of doing business.
items.title: RBI clarifies forex reporting rules for services exports, with a per-remittance threshold

items.summary: The article argues, without citing a source, that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's alleged China ties have opened opportunities for Indian tycoons to become trusted custodians of Western AI technology. It reports that Reliance Industries has committed 10 trillion rupees ($107 billion) over seven years to an AI hub and the Adani Group plans $100 billion in data-center investment by 2035, with both groups developing large green-energy projects in Kutch; these figures are stated as commitments or plans rather than completed outcomes. The piece attributes framing of US policy to it: Washington's "Pax Silica" initiative under Secretary Marco Rubio is described as aimed at China-proofing the AI supply chain, and India joined the San Francisco Declaration while being absent from a list of high-risk destinations for chip diversion.
